messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Rajesh

Rajesh was thirty-four when the moment that would unmake his sense of himself occurred on a Tuesday afternoon in late September. He had been driving for Apex Logistics for six years, a reliable operator with a clean record and the kind of quiet competence that earned him steady routes through the suburbs of Phoenix. On that particular day, he was making a delivery to a residential neighborhood, navigating a street he had driven a hundred times before. The sun was bright, the road was clear, and Rajesh was thinking about his wife Priya's suggestion that they finally book the trip to visit his parents in Gujarat—a conversation they'd been postponing for months. He turned onto Maple Street at the usual speed, glancing in his mirror as he always did, and that was when he saw the boy.

The child, no more than seven or eight, had darted from between two parked cars. Rajesh's foot found the brake almost before his mind registered what was happening, but the truck's momentum carried him forward. He heard the sickening impact, the sound of breaking glass from the windshield, the screams from the sidewalk. The boy—whose name he would later learn was Marcus—lay beneath the front wheel, his leg bent at an angle that made Rajesh's stomach turn. The paramedics arrived within minutes. Marcus survived, but he would need surgery, months of rehabilitation, and would walk with a limp for the rest of his childhood. Rajesh had not been speeding. The police report confirmed he was within the limit. None of that mattered.

In the weeks that followed, Rajesh replayed those seconds countless times, each replay a fresh accusation against himself. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt immovable, that he should have been more vigilant, that a more careful driver would have anticipated the danger even though the boy had emerged from a blind spot. He tormented himself with the thought that he could have done more in those fractions of a second—braked harder, swerved differently, somehow prevented what happened. The guilt was not a feeling that came and went; it was a permanent fixture in his chest, a weight that made it difficult to breathe. What frightened Rajesh most was the conviction that he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened, that the failure to protect Marcus would define him forever. He had failed in the most fundamental way—as a responsible person, as someone who should have known better, as a man who was supposed to keep others safe.

His marriage began to fracture under the strain. Priya would find him in the garage at two in the morning, sitting in the cab of his truck with the engine off, staring at nothing. She tried to tell him that it was an accident, that he was not responsible, but her reassurances only deepened his conviction that she did not understand the magnitude of what he had done. Rajesh believed the event had happened because of the way he had acted—his decision to turn onto Maple Street, his speed, his lack of absolute vigilance. He had made choices, and those choices had consequences that a child would carry for life. Priya eventually stopped trying to comfort him and began sleeping in the guest room, exhausted by the weight of his self-condemnation.

Four months after the accident, Rajesh finally came to his first therapy appointment, referred by his family doctor who had noticed his weight loss and the tremor in his hands. He sat in the chair with his hands clasped so tightly his knuckles were white, unable to make eye contact. When asked why he was there, he said only, "I need to understand how I'm supposed to live with what I've done." His voice was hollow, and in it was the sound of a man who had concluded that the answer might be that he was not.
